idiom_name: block with yield (or a &blk parameter captured as a Proc)
implementation_notes: Ruby's block is the local idiom that replaces a stored callback object: the method yields to the block immediately, so no callback type and no registration are involved (Enumerable methods, File.open { |f| ... }). The block becomes an ordinary callback only when it must outlive the call - capture it with an &blk parameter into a Proc, or build one with Proc.new, lambda or method(:name) - and the proc-versus-lambda difference decides its semantics. Asynchronous completion in Ruby is threads, fibers or a library (Async, concurrent-ruby, EventMachine) rather than a callback field; a class responding to call remains the right shape for a listener-like object whose lifecycle the application manages.
code_sketch:
class Fetcher
  def fetch(url, &on_done)                # the block is the callback
    Thread.new do
      body = Net::HTTP.get(URI(url))
      on_done.call(body, nil)
    rescue StandardError => e
      on_done.call(nil, e)                # exactly one completion
    end
  end

  def on(event, &handler) = (@handlers ||= {})[event] = handler   # stored callback
end
pitfalls: proc/Proc.new returns from the defining method when invoked, while lambda returns locally and alone checks arity - the classic block semantics trap.
A stored block closes over its binding, so keeping Procs in a registry keeps every local in that binding alive for the process lifetime.
MRI's GVL hides races in callbacks that touch shared state; on JRuby or TruffleRuby the same code races unless the state is synchronized.
Calling a stored handler after its owner is gone raises NoMethodError on a dead object or silently mutates stale state, because unregistering is always manual.
